text: The camera does not move, and the man in the bed is trying to hand his daughter something that will not fit into words. Héctor Faver builds his eighty-two minutes out of that attempt: monologues from a camp survivor near the end of his life, then his wife, then his daughter, each taking a turn at the same errand. Between them runs the archive everyone has already seen, the standard reels of atrocity shown so often they slide off the eye. The friction is deliberate. Public footage is exact and belongs to nobody; the dying man's account is imprecise and belongs only to him; the daughter has to take delivery of both at once. Argentina, 1992, in Spanish, half a century downstream of the events, at the point when the people who were there began to run out of time.

A seat that cannot be lost is a strange place to spend three years filming a campaign. Daniel Draper does it anyway, staying with the activists on the safest Labour ground in the country as they work under the banner of Jeremy Corbyn's For The Many manifesto, across what the film treats as the decisive years for the party. The local result is arithmetic, settled before anyone knocks on a door, which frees the eighty-nine minutes for something harder to photograph: what people do with their evenings once belief has to be organised into tasks. Meetings, arguments over wording, the same faces in the same rooms. A manifesto is a promise made in the plural, and Draper watches the few who take that plural personally, in one town, while the party it belongs to argues with itself elsewhere.

Every image here was exposed by someone else, decades ago, for purposes that had nothing to do with this film. Maciej J. Drygas assembles Pociągi out of what the twentieth century left behind on film, and hangs a line of Kafka over the whole of it: there is hope, an infinite amount of hope, but not for us. Eighty minutes of other people's Europe, gathered into a crowd rather than a story, the hopes and appetites and disasters all anonymous now. The organising figure is the machine in the title, which carried that century's populations toward work, toward holidays, and toward places nobody chose. Poland is where it was made, and the last of those needs no underlining. The faces in this footage were filmed by people who expected the century to end differently.

For its first ten minutes the film will not say what happened; it lets a man smoking beside a broken window and the far-off sound of ships' horns do the saying. Then the road, traffic keeping its ordinary pace, rubble still smoldering at the shoulder, helicopters turning overhead: the 4 August 2020 explosion at the Port of Beirut, reached from the side rather than announced. Karim Kassem has sixty-four minutes and gives the first of them to aftermath as texture, damage treated as furniture, sound doing the work an establishing shot usually does. Nothing in the delay is coy. A city that has absorbed an event of that size does not introduce it either, and Kassem keeps the city's pace instead of the pace of explanation.

Three magazine reporters, one city, and a political scene that keeps writing their copy for them. Wynn Lau Chun-Fai's ninety-seven minutes take Hong Kong politics as raw material for comedy, which is a decision about form before it is a decision about targets: a joke can point at a public figure without having to prove a case against him, and it can run in a magazine. The film stays with the profession rather than the policy, with the chase for a line, the deadline, the readership's appetite for the ridiculous. Reporters make useful comic leads because the job is to be in the room and then describe it badly, at speed, for money. The year is 2016, and the material was arriving faster than three reporters could file it.

Soraya is sixteen and makes drawings and sculptures that are far past competent and not at all reassuring. She is Afghan, she lives in Iran, and for five years, most of the way through her adolescence, she has been trying to reach her mother in Austria. Mehrdad Oskouei gives his seventy-six minutes not to a departure but to the years that surround one: a life arranged around an address in another country, and around the waiting such an arrangement requires. The work is the second subject and possibly the first. A teenager with that much control of her materials is already saying where she stands, and the discipline of the film is to let the objects speak before the circumstances do, so that Soraya remains a maker with a problem rather than a problem that happens to make things.

A British picture made in 1943, with the war still unfinished, in which the great friendship of a career officer's life is with a German. The present tense of the film is small and humiliating: General Candy, handed a squad of men who consider him a relic and are not entirely wrong. Everything else is retrieval. The Boer War, then the earlier world war, a young officer with fine manners and a great deal of luck, and three women, each of whom rearranges him. Michael Powell takes 163 minutes because obsolescence cannot be felt in ninety; it has to be watched accumulating. What the film declines to do is the interesting part. It had every opportunity to turn the German into a lesson and instead made him the man Candy misses, which in Britain in 1943 was not a neutral thing to put on a screen.

A snowball fight staged with maps, flanks and a chain of command: the first thing Abel Gance establishes is that his subject was rehearsing. From there the film runs past seven hours, out of Corsica and into the Revolution, where a storm at sea is cut against a storm in a hall of shouting men until the two become one weather system. Rhyme is the method, and Gance trusts it further than any argument he might have made instead. The span closes on the Italian campaign of 1797, early, which keeps the picture about ascent rather than aftermath. Silent, in 1927, it had to find visible equivalents for oratory, for panic, for a crowd changing its mind mid-sentence. The 425 minutes are not grandeur for its own sake; length is how a life is shown gathering speed, and the speed is the thesis.

A man who has made his living with a gun asks a homesteading family for work, and means it. What follows is pressure applied from outside, a rancher who regards the valley as his, settlers who have built on it, a grievance too old to be talked down, while inside the house the days go on being about chores and meals. George Stevens spends much of his 118 minutes there, on the routine, so that when the film finally moves it registers as an interruption rather than a delivery. It took the Academy's award for colour cinematography, and the prize is legible in the frame: not prettiness but depth, the fact that a rider can be very far off and still be present in the scene. The awkwardness at the centre is domestic. A household adjusts around a newcomer, and nobody will name the adjustment aloud.

The name on the bill was Madame Satã, and the man who answered to it had already been half a dozen other things. João Francisco dos Santos: son of slaves, ex-convict, street fighter, lover of men, and the person a number of Rio's unwanted called father. Karim Aïnouz keeps to the 1930s and to the hillside districts above a city that preferred not to look up, and he refuses to let any single one of those descriptions win the argument. The cabaret is filmed as work rather than escape, a matter of costume, rehearsal, and a room that has to be held. Abraccine's hundred best Brazilian films includes it, though the reason to watch sits nearer the ground: 105 minutes in the company of a body that is hungry, tired, and never once arranged into a moral.

There is no honest way to describe this film in a single register. D.W. Griffith built 193 minutes in 1915 around two families, Northern abolitionists and Southern landowners, braided them through the war, then carried that domestic sympathy into Reconstruction South Carolina, where the picture asks an audience to take the founding of the Ku Klux Klan as deliverance. The craft is not in dispute and neither is the poison; they are one object, which is exactly the difficulty. It sits in the National Film Registry, and it is watched now the way a document is watched: for the joins, for the point in the machinery where feeling is converted into instruction, for the evidence of what an audience in 1915 was willing to be told about itself.

A musical that keeps stopping to look at the damage, then goes back to the number. George Cukor runs 196 minutes, roughly twice what the story needs, and the surplus is the point: songs are allowed to go long, the quiet after them longer, and two careers are watched passing each other in the same corridors on the same schedule. One is being assembled, a singer given a name, a face, an audience. The other is coming apart from age and drink, and the film refuses to make either process especially dramatic; both are work and weather. What it knows best is the machinery around them, a studio's habit of manufacturing people, and the peculiar courtesy of a business that goes on smiling at a man while it arranges his replacement.
